lead: Fault tolerance is the property that a cloud service keeps working when parts of it break. A cloud never asks whether a server will fail; it assumes failure, detects it with a heartbeat, and moves the work to a replica. Every provider turns that into a promise: a recovery time objective (how long until service returns) and a recovery point objective (how much data may be lost). UPI switches, ticketing sites and payment gateways are built this way, and the promise is what the customer actually buys.
prereq: You need: 4.1 for chunks and metadata, 4.2 for replica placement, and 4.3 for quorum reads and writes.

sections.h3: Faults and four kinds of redundancy

blocks.text: Only a few universities teach this chapter in depth. A fault is a defect; a failure is the visible loss of service. Cloud design assumes every disk, server, switch and zone will fail, so it never asks whether, only when.

items: Omission: a message is dropped or a step skipped.
Timing: the answer arrives too late.
Byzantine: the node answers wrongly, sometimes on purpose.

blocks.text: Redundancy is the cure. Hardware redundancy adds a second server. Software redundancy adds a second process or a retry. Time redundancy repeats the operation. Information redundancy adds check bits or extra copies of the data. A second replica on separate hardware buys hardware and information redundancy at once, which is why clouds lean on it.
Detection is the other half. A heartbeat is a small periodic message; the monitor declares a node dead after k missed beats. Large k means slow detection, small k means false alarms.

sections.h3: Replication models and their consistency cost

blocks.text: Primary-backup. One replica, the primary, takes all writes and holds a lease, a time-bounded permission to be primary. It forwards each write to the backups. When the heartbeat stops, the monitor waits for the lease to expire, then promotes a backup. The lease stops two nodes from both believing they are primary.

Quorum. With N replicas a write must reach W of them and a read must contact R. The rule below makes every read set overlap every write set, so a read sees the latest write. With N = 3, W = 3 and R = 1 reads are cheap and writes are slow.

blocks.where: N is the number of replicas; W is the number of replicas that must acknowledge a write; R is the number of replicas a read must contact.

blocks.text: Chain replication. The head takes the write and passes it along a chain; the tail answers reads. Writes stay ordered and reads are cheap, but a mid-chain failure stalls the pipeline.
Multi-master. Every replica accepts writes and merges later: highest availability, weakest consistency. Good for carts and counters, not for balances.

sections.h3: Business continuity: RTO, RPO, backups and drills

blocks.text: Business continuity is fault tolerance written as a customer promise, fixed by two numbers. RTO (recovery time objective) is the longest acceptable time to restore service. RPO (recovery point objective) is the acceptable data loss, measured in time.

Backup types. Full copies everything. Incremental copies changes since the last backup of any kind. Differential copies changes since the last full. Restoring an incremental chain needs the last full plus every increment.

Sites. A hot site runs in parallel and takes over in minutes. A warm site is provisioned but needs current data loaded. A cold site is floor space and contracts; recovery takes days. A runbook is the written recovery procedure; a drill is its rehearsal. An untested runbook is a guess.
Allowed downtime per month = (1 − A) × 43,200 minutes
blocks.where: A is availability as a fraction (99.9% → 0.999); 43,200 = 30 × 24 × 60, the minutes in a 30-day month.

spec.aria: Two timelines of snapshot ticks, hourly and every 15 minutes, with a crash at minute 59 showing the data lost in each, and an arrow for the 60-minute recovery time.

examples.question: A service promises 99.9% availability with RPO 15 minutes and RTO 1 hour. A 30-day month has 30 × 24 × 60 minutes. (a) How much downtime per month does 99.9% allow, and how much does 99.99% allow? (b) Is an hourly snapshot enough for the RPO? (c) What does the 1-hour RTO demand?
steps: 99.9% availability leaves 1 − 0.999 = 0.001 of the month unavailable.
An hourly snapshot loses up to 60 minutes of data, more than the 15-minute RPO, so snapshot or ship the transaction log every 15 minutes or less.
The 1-hour RTO is a separate requirement: the runbook must restore service within 60 minutes.
examples.answer: 99.9% allows 43.2 minutes of downtime per month (4.32 minutes at 99.99%), and hourly snapshots break the 15-minute RPO, so snapshots must run at least every 15 minutes.

traps: Swapping RTO and RPO: RTO is time to restore service, RPO is data lost measured in time.
Calling three replicas a backup. A bad write or a delete reaches every replica instantly; only a point-in-time copy survives human error or corruption.
Adding replicas inside one rack or zone: they share a failure domain, so availability does not rise.
Breaking the quorum rule: W + R must be greater than N, or a read may miss the latest write.
Reading 99.9% as 0.1 minute per month. It is 0.1% of 43,200 minutes = 43.2 minutes.

quiz.a: RTO is the longest acceptable time to restore service; RPO is the acceptable data loss, measured in time.

quiz.q: Why does the primary hold a lease?
quiz.a: The lease is time-bounded permission to act as primary. The monitor waits for it to expire before promoting a backup, so two nodes cannot both accept writes.

quiz.q: Why is a heartbeat timeout a trade-off?
quiz.a: Small k detects failure fast but declares live nodes dead; large k avoids false alarms but stretches the outage.

quiz.q: N = 3. Give one valid (W, R) pair that is read-optimised and one that is write-optimised.
quiz.a: Read-optimised: W = 3, R = 1, since 3 + 1 > 3. Write-optimised: W = 1, R = 3, since 1 + 3 > 3.

quiz.q: A service promises 99.95% availability. Find the allowed downtime in a 30-day month.
quiz.a: 43,200 minutes in the month; unavailable fraction 0.0005; 0.0005 × 43,200 = 21.6 minutes per month.

quiz.q: A team keeps three replicas in one rack and says it has disaster recovery. What is wrong?
quiz.a: One rack or zone failure kills all three, so they share a failure domain; replicas must cross failure domains. Also, replicas copy bad writes and deletes, so a point-in-time backup is still needed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry now rehearses failure on purpose: chaos engineering injects node and zone kills in production to test the runbook rather than trust it. Conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs) let multi-master replicas merge without a coordinator, which is why offline-first apps sync so easily. Cloud providers publish per-region error budgets, and teams spend them on releases. Search next for failure domains, chaos engineering, CRDTs and error budgets.
